The White-crested spadebill (Platyrinchus platyrhynchos) is a small suboscine passerine inhabiting the understory of lowland Amazonian forests. Newly hatched altricial nestlings emerge from eggs incubated for approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days] at a nest temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], a developmental duration typical of Tyrannidae given their modest egg sizes. At hatching, these nestlings weigh just 1.3 grams [Wwb = 1.3 grams], reflecting the extremely altricial state of the neonates, which are nearly naked and entirely dependent on parental brooding and provisioning. This initial mass is notably low compared to the ultimate wet weight attained by adult females, which reaches approximately 13 grams [Wwi = approximately 13 grams], indicating a roughly ten-fold increase in body mass over the nestling and fledgling periods. The energetic demands of this rapid growth are substantial, and field studies using flow-through respirometry on inactive, post-absorptive individuals under controlled thermal conditions have documented a maximum basal metabolic rate of 54.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 54.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], reflecting the metabolic ceiling for this species.

The fledging period is notably brief; young spadebills achieve their first flight and depart the nest at 12 days after hatching [tx = 12 days after hatching], a remarkably short developmental interval that may be an adaptation to reduce nest predation risk in the exposed understory strata where the domed nests are constructed at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Reproductive output in the White-crested spadebill is constrained by its single-brooded breeding system. Females typically produce one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], laying between 2 and 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 2 and 5 eggs per clutch], with the modal clutch size being three eggs. This modest annual reproductive output is balanced by a relatively extended potential lifespan. The combination of a single annual clutch with a high adult survival rate suggests a slow life-history strategy typical of tropical understory insectivores.

Comparative physiological data from related Tyrannidae species offer context for understanding the metabolic and reproductive traits of the White-crested spadebill. The resting oxygen consumption of 54.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 54.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour] measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] is consistent with values reported for other small-bodied flycatchers, falling within the expected range for a 13 gram [Wwi = 13 gram] passerine when adjusted for the allometric scaling of basal metabolic rate. The 36-day interval to puberty (36 days after hatching) [tp = 36 days after hatching] is also compressed relative to temperate-zone congeners, possibly an adaptation to high juvenile mortality at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

The thermal sensitivity of metabolic rate in Platyrinchus platyrhynchos, as indicated by the basal oxygen consumption of 54.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 54.55 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], suggests a narrow thermoneutral zone typical of small-bodied tropical passerines. Unlike temperate Tyrannidae that exhibit pronounced seasonal metabolic adjustments, this species appears to maintain a relatively constant metabolic expenditure year-round, likely due to the stable ambient temperatures of its lowland forest habitat. The modest body mass of 13 grams [Wwi = 13 grams] in adult females is consistent with predictions from allometric equations linking mass to metabolic scope, and the brief 12-day incubation period (12 days) [ab = 12 days] at 34 °C [T = 34 °C] may be facilitated by the high metabolic capacity of the incubating female, who must allocate sufficient energy to maintain optimal egg temperatures while also meeting her own maintenance requirements.
